The lesion started as a small painless mass on the right lateral aspect of the tongue, which gradually grew and subsequently ulcerated
No history of trauma or tongue bite preceding the lesion
Patient denied consuming tobacco or alcohol regularly
Medical history includes well-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus for 2 years with oral hypoglycemic agents
Single well-defined ulcer measuring 2 × 2 cm on the right lateral aspect of tongue with a clean base and irregular and elevated heaped-up margins
No underlying induration, friability, or bleeding on manipulation
Dense diffuse infiltrate of lymphocytes, histiocytes, epithelioid cells, giant cells, plasma cells, eosinophils, and neutrophils
Many histiocytes and giant cells contained intracellular yeasts with a surrounding halo
Special stains (Grocott-Gomori methenamine-silver nitrate and periodic acid–Schiff) highlighted fungal forms
Fungal culture on Sabouraud dextrose agar was negative
HIV-1 and HIV-2 serologic testing were negative

erythema appeared in the area irradiated with UV-A 48 hours afterwards

The presence of severe cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, along with palatal myoclonus and other symptoms, is consistent with Olivopontocerebellar Atrophy, a subtype of Multiple System Atrophy.
The combination of hypometric saccades, bradykinesia, mild rigidity, and palatal myoclonus, along with severe cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, is also consistent with Progressive Supranuclear Palsy.
The presence of bradykinesia, mild rigidity, and palatal myoclonus, along with severe cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, is also consistent with Corticobasal Degeneration.

facts.raw_span: A 14-year-old girl presented with a 6-year history of a photosensitive eruption involving her face, neck, trunk, and extremities
Her symptoms began at age 8 years

She had previously tried multiple medications including systemic steroids, hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, tofacitinib, rituximab, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), with minimal improvement
Violaceous erythema on forehead and midface
Diffuse poikiloderma involving upper chest, anterolateral thighs, and extensor arms
Erythematous, flat-topped papules on extensor joints of hands
Nailfold examination showed dilated capillary loops, capillary dropout, and ragged cuticles
Elevated serum IFN-β levels (8 pg/mL, normal ≤2 pg/mL)
Presence of anti-TIF-1γ autoantibodies
Radiographic evidence of myositis
Confirmatory skin biopsy performed

concepts.why: The patient's photosensitive eruption, violaceous erythema, diffuse poikiloderma, erythematous papules, and nailfold changes are consistent with dermatomyositis, and the presence of anti-TIF-1γ autoantibodies, elevated serum IFN-β levels, and radiographic evidence of myositis support this diagnosis.

The patient's photosensitive eruption, violaceous erythema, diffuse poikiloderma, and erythematous papules could be seen in lupus erythematosus, and the presence of anti-TIF-1γ autoantibodies and elevated serum IFN-β levels are also consistent with this diagnosis.
The patient's combination of dermatomyositis-like skin changes, myositis, and presence of anti-TIF-1γ autoantibodies could be seen in mixed connective tissue disease.

milia and a few erosions with partially detached epidermis were identified
no abnormalities of the mucous membranes, nails, hair, or teeth
no extracutaneous involvement was observed
Multiple pruritic erythematous to violaceous lichenified papules and plaques on the left shin
Close-up examination revealed erosion with partially detached epidermis and multiple milia
Histopathologic examination revealed dermoepidermal separation
Histopathologic examination revealed several milia in the superficial dermis
Whole-exome sequencing identified a novel heterozygous missense variant, c.6832G>T, p.Gly2278Trp, in COL7A1 (NM_000094)
Sanger sequencing confirmed cosegregation of this variant

concepts.why: The patient's presentation of progressive, itchy erythematous to violaceous papules and plaques, along with histopathologic findings of dermoepidermal separation and milia, is consistent with Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa, and the identification of a novel heterozygous missense variant in COL7A1 further supports this diagnosis.
The patient's severe skin manifestations, including erosions and milia, along with the genetic findings, are consistent with Recessive Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa, a subtype of DEB.
